name: Yusuf Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Yusuf, thanks for doing this. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and nothing you say will be published with your name. Can you tell me what a normal working day looks like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a machine operator at a family-run engineering firm that makes hydraulic fittings, the brass and steel connectors that go on diggers and tractors. I run two CNC lathes, which are lathes controlled by a computer program, so I load bar stock, start the program, measure the first parts with a micrometer and keep an eye on tool wear. I'm still junior, so the programmers write the programs and I just run them, but I'm trying to learn that side. I share a flat with my mate Tariq about ten minutes away by bike.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are you trying to learn it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mostly at night with an AI chat app, honestly. I paste in a bit of program and ask it to explain each line, then I check it against what the lathe actually does the next day. I'm doing a free online course on PLCs too, which are the little computers that control a lot of factory machines. My supervisor, Hughes, laughs at me, but he's also started asking me to look things up for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's a bit disappointing, actually. I'd probably post a joke about all the people who told me to stop playing with chatbots. But I'd also say it shows the bosses' promises about robots replacing everyone were overblown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be a bit let down. I like this stuff. But it also means the normal route works: learn programming, become a setter, then a programmer, and get paid properly for it. That's a decent life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the AI apps to learn, finish the PLC course, and ask Hughes in the first year if I can start writing simple programs under supervision. I'd keep saving like now, about three months of bills sitting there, and maybe start a proper evening course at the college.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, like when a match you were excited about ends nil-nil.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would it put you off using the AI tools if they turned out to be mostly hype?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not at all. Even if AI is just a better textbook, it's made me learn faster. I went from not knowing what a G-code was to fixing a small offset problem in six months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you push for, if anything, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay. If AI makes us each a bit faster but wages stay the same, the owners keep the difference. I'd want the union to bargain on that. We don't have a strong union at our place, which is half the problem.

S0.say: That's a bit disappointing, and I'd post a joke about people who told me to stop playing with chatbots. It also shows the bosses' promises about replacing everyone were overblown.
S0.think: I'd be a bit let down because I like this stuff. But the normal route still works: learn programming, become a setter, then a programmer and get paid for it.
S0.do: Finishes the PLC course and keeps using AI apps to study programs at night. Asks his supervisor within a year to write simple programs under supervision. Keeps his three months of savings and considers an evening college course.
S0.feel: Calm and a little flat, like an anticlimax.
S0.quote: A bit flat, like when a match you were excited about ends nil-nil.
S0.fieldNote: Yusuf is the rare person who'd be disappointed by a plateau. He already uses AI daily as a tutor and credits it with speeding up his learning. Even here his politics show: he wants any productivity gain shared through bargaining, and he regrets the weak union at his firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good if we do it right. Machines should take the boring bits and workers should get trained and paid more for running them. I'd be loud online that companies need to share the gains, not just cut heads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd do well out of this. My job running lathes shrinks, but someone has to set up and program the robot cells, and I'm already learning that. The worry isn't me, it's the lads who won't touch it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd ask Hughes to put me forward for any training on the new kit. I'd sign up for the college's automation certificate in the evenings, and if our firm didn't invest I'd apply to the bigger plant across town that's already got robot cells. I'd keep some savings back in case the move meant a pay dip at first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited, a little nervous. Like the first day at a new job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Danny. He's thirty-five, he's good with his hands, but he hates screens. He says AI is for people who can't think. He'd be the first one they move to sweeping up, and he'd be too proud to ask for help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do for him, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to sit with him, show him the stuff I use. He'd probably tell me where to go the first time. Maybe the third time he'd say yes. You can't force it on people.

S1.say: This is good if we do it right: machines take the boring bits and workers get trained and paid more. Companies need to share the gains, not just cut heads.
S1.think: I'd do well out of this, because someone has to set up and program the robot cells and I'm already learning. The worry is the lads who won't touch it.
S1.do: Asks to be put forward for training on new equipment in the first month. Starts an evening automation certificate at the local college. Applies to a bigger plant with robot cells if his firm doesn't invest, keeping savings in reserve for a possible pay dip.
S1.quote: He says AI is for people who can't think.
S1.fieldNote: This is Yusuf's best-case world and he knows it. He's willing to change employer if his family-run firm is slow. His concern for Danny, a proud colleague who hates screens, keeps his optimism from sounding smug.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this has to be public. If machines can do all the work, the gains can't sit in three companies. I'd back anything that puts money in people's pockets straight away, a basic income, a robot tax, whatever moves fastest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, this one actually scares me. Everything I've been learning is the next rung up, and in this picture there isn't a next rung, the AI programs the robots itself. I'd be twenty-nine with skills that were worth something for about a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save every spare penny and get to six months of bills if I could. I'd try to make some money while things are still messy, maybe setting up AI tools and robots for small workshops that don't understand them, on weekends. And I'd join the union and get involved in campaigning, because I can't fix this on my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. A bit betrayed, almost, by the thing I liked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is very short. What does that short warning change for you specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That being early stops mattering. With five or ten years, being the guy who learned first gives you a head start. With two years, everyone ends up in the same place, just me a few months later than Danny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. Would you keep using it in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using it, because it's the fastest way to understand what's happening. That sounds strange, I know. You don't stop reading the weather forecast because there's a storm coming.

S2.say: This has to be public: if machines do all the work, the gains can't sit in three companies. I'd back whatever puts money in people's pockets fastest, like a basic income or a robot tax.
S2.think: This one scares me, because there's no next rung when AI programs the robots itself. I'd be twenty-nine with skills that were worth something for about a year.
S2.do: Saves every spare penny, aiming for six months of bills. Earns extra on weekends setting up AI tools and robots for small workshops while things are messy. Joins the union and campaigns for fast public support.
S2.feel: Alarmed, and slightly betrayed by the technology he enjoys.
S2.quote: In this picture there isn't a next rung, the AI programs the robots itself.
S2.fieldNote: This is where his adaptability stops protecting him, and he sees it clearly: being early only helps if there's time. His weekend side-income idea is opportunistic and realistic. His weather-forecast line about still using AI was a neat way to hold the contradiction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get the rules right if people start now: who owns the machines, how people get paid, what school's for. I'd be posting about it and probably bothering my local councillor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd get maybe three or four good years as a robot technician before AGI catches up. That's real money, and real experience. It'd buy me time to work out what comes after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the automation certificate in the first year and move to the plant with robot cells by year two, for the higher pay. I'd save half of the pay rise. And I'd keep doing small setup jobs for workshops on the side, because that builds contacts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a busy way. I'd be doing too much to sit and worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'what comes after'. What do you imagine that is?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably helping people get through it. Like teaching, or working for the union or the council on retraining. If machines do the work, the useful thing left is helping people cope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a tension between building robots for a living and campaigning for workers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tariq would say I'm a hypocrite for working on the robots and campaigning against job losses. Maybe. But I'd rather be the one in the room who cares what happens to people.

S3.say: Five years is enough to get the rules right if people start now: who owns the machines, how people get paid, what school is for. I'd post about it and bother my local councillor.
S3.think: I'd get three or four good years as a robot technician before AGI catches up. That's real money and experience, and time to work out what comes after.
S3.do: Finishes the automation certificate in year one and moves to a plant with robot cells by year two. Saves half of the pay rise. Keeps doing setup jobs for small workshops on the side and lobbies his councillor.
S3.feel: Anxious but too busy to dwell on it.
S3.quote: I'd rather be the one in the room who cares what happens to people.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives his strategy a window again, and his mood lifts with it. He plans to bank part of a higher wage, showing he treats the technician job as temporary. He owned the tension between building robots and campaigning without getting defensive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a real chance to build something fair. I'd say let's use it for shorter working weeks, public stakes in the robot firms, and free retraining. I'd be one of those annoying people in every comment section.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd have a good run. Technician, maybe programmer, maybe even a small business installing systems. Then at the end I'd still be thirty-seven and facing the same question everyone else does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the automation certificate, then a part-time engineering diploma over three or four years. I'd move to a better-paying job when I was ready, not in a rush. I'd keep campaigning on the side, maybe stand for a union role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the end of the road, but pretty good about the next ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned standing for a union role. Is that something you'd really do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, actually. I'd want to be in a position to say something useful when it arrives, not just shout. Ten years of working inside automation would give me that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does any of this change your plans outside work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want a partner and maybe kids within those ten years, honestly. My mum keeps asking. I'd rather do it while there's still a normal job market, not wait until after.

S4.say: Ten years is a real chance to build something fair: shorter weeks, public stakes in robot firms and free retraining. I'd be in every comment section about it.
S4.think: I'd have a good run as a technician, maybe a programmer or a small business owner. Then at thirty-seven I'd face the same question everyone else does.
S4.do: Completes the automation certificate, then a part-time engineering diploma over three or four years. Moves to a better-paid job when ready rather than in a rush. Stands for a union role and campaigns on the side.
S4.feel: Good about the next ten years, uneasy about the end of the road.
S4.quote: Then at the end I'd still be thirty-seven and facing the same question everyone else does.
S4.fieldNote: The long warning lets him pace himself and add a diploma, but he never pretends adaptability saves him at the end. He wants a voice inside the change, through a union role. Wanting to settle down before 2036 came up without prompting about family.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it takes away the one advantage I've got, which is being early. What would help is the government acting fast, an income for everyone that doesn't depend on a job, and some public ownership of the systems doing the work. And free courses that aren't just about getting another job, because there may not be one.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether people like me actually want to stop working. I don't. I like making something with tight tolerances and measuring it and it's right. I'd want something to do with my hands even if nobody paid me.

headlineQuote: I like making something with tight tolerances and measuring it and it's right.
portrait: Yusuf is a 27-year-old junior CNC lathe operator at a family-run hydraulic fittings firm, sharing a flat with his friend Tariq and teaching himself programming at night with an AI chat app. He's progressive and adaptive: excited by automation, he plans to become a robot technician while campaigning for public ownership and fair sharing of the gains. A plateau would leave him a bit flat and steady change would suit him, but fast AGI alarms him because being early stops counting. With five or ten years he plans in stages and banks money, without pretending it saves him at the end.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it takes away his only advantage, which is learning the new technology early.
whatWouldHelp: Fast government action with an income that doesn't depend on a job, public ownership of the systems doing the work, and free courses that aren't only about finding another job.
